newsitem.title: FRANCE: Food firms to stress safety first at Paris fair.
newsitem.headline: Food firms to stress safety first at Paris fair.

text.p: Consumers' concerns about what they eat will dominate Europe's leading international food fair in Paris next week at a time when consumer confidence has been badly shaken by the scare over mad cow disease.
"Food quality and safety will be at the core of the International Food Salon (SIAL) this year," the event's organiser Victor Scherrer told Reuters on Friday.
The 4,000 exhibitors from 83 countries meeting between October 20 and October 24 face consumers who "want to know what they are putting on their plate," Scherrer said.

"Consumers want food that is tasty, but also healthy. They want to know where the product is coming from, what its ingredients are...The mad cow scare has increased the need to track down the origin of the product," he said.
A comparative study on "food habits in eight countries" by the Ipsos agency showed that price, taste and food safety would be the main criteria for consumers for the next five years.
Food producers are paying close attention to these trends because they are fighting a global battle for market share in a lucrative and fast growing sector.
In 1994, trade in processed food products accounted for two-thirds of a world agri-food market of $366 billion francs against half in 1984.
Producers are also aware that consumers are increasingly willing to spend more on products they think will be good for their health or will just make them feel good.
Illustrating this trend, the market for organic products is exploding in France where 150 new companies started up business last year.

Food giants like Danone have made health issues the core of their marketing strategies. Italian oil giant Carapelli is introducing at the SIAL fair a new low-cholesterol oil Leciviva made from soybean sprouts.
The mad cow scare accelerated a shift in consumers' habits that started in early 1995, making the fair an ideal forum for producers eager to restore consumers' confidence in meat products.
France was the first nation to ban imports of British beef after Britain announced in March a possible link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and a fatal disease in humans.
National meat board OFIVAL expects beef comsumption in France may fall by 10-15 percent in 1996 over 1995.
Foreign meat producers will outnumber French at the fair, SIAL data showed. But Ofival will be at SIAL to tell consumers it is safe and healthy to eat French meat.
